Hatchlings of the Green whip snake emerge from parchment-shelled eggs with a snout–vent length of approximately 25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 25 centimeters], a value typical for colubrid neonates that must immediately begin foraging for small lizards and insects. This initial size constrains their early predation options, as they can only subdue prey items smaller than their own head diameter. Within their first weeks of life, these young individuals undergo a period of rapid somatic growth, progressively shifting from an exclusive diet of arthropods toward larger vertebrate prey as their gape size increases. The leathery-shelled eggs are deposited in concealed, humid microhabitats such as rotting logs or deep leaf litter, where the stable thermal environment facilitates successful embryonic development. After eclosion, the yolk-sac larva stage is brief, as the residual yolk is rapidly absorbed and the juvenile snake begins its exotrophic transition within days of emergence. Field studies across Italy and southern France have consistently recorded this hatchling length, suggesting it is a conserved trait that reflects an optimal balance between parental investment in egg size and the survival demands faced by newly emerged snakes in a resource-variable Mediterranean landscape.

As adults, the Green whip snake exhibits pronounced sexual size dimorphism, with females attaining a maximum snout–vent length of 108 centimeters [Li = 108 centimeters] while males regularly reach a larger ultimate length of 120 centimeters [Li = 120 centimeters]. This difference in body size likely reflects divergent selective pressures operating on each sex: larger male body size may confer advantages in male-male combat during the breeding season, where individuals engage in ritualized wrestling contests for access to gravid females. Conversely, the slightly smaller female size may be linked to the energetic demands of egg production, as a moderately elongated body cavity still accommodates a substantial clutch volume without incurring excessive locomotor costs. These asymptotic lengths are documented in museum specimen series collected over decades, and comparative data from congeneric species suggest that such dimorphism is widespread within the genus Hierophis. The maximum recorded adult mass for a snake of this body plan, based on morphometric scaling relationships with similarly proportioned colubrids, is estimated at 1678 grams [Wwi = 1678 grams], a value that underscores the species' robust build relative to other Mediterranean whip snakes.

Reproductive activity in the Green whip snake is tightly linked to seasonal thermal conditions, and under controlled laboratory settings maintained at 18 °C [T = 18 °C], females have been observed to produce clutches ranging from 4 to 15 eggs per litter [N_R_i = 4 to 15 eggs per litter], with the frequency of reproduction ranging from one to approximately four clutches per year [F_R_i = approximately four clutches per year]. This reproductive output is moderate for a colubrid of this body size, and the annual single-clutch strategy is common among temperate-zone viperine and colubrine snakes that experience a short, resource-rich active season. The maximum rate of egg production under these stable thermal conditions, integrating both clutch size and frequency, corresponds to an annual output that allows females to replenish their somatic reserves between breeding events. Given the constraints of a Mediterranean climate with hot, dry summers, the ability to produce only one well-provisioned clutch per year likely enhances offspring quality at the expense of total fecundity, a trade-off frequently observed in oviparous reptiles inhabiting seasonal environments.

Longevity records for the Green whip snake, derived from mark-recapture studies in central Italian populations, indicate that individuals can survive for 33 years [am = 33 years] when maintained under optimal captive conditions at a constant ambient temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. This exceptional lifespan is among the greatest documented for any European colubrid and likely reflects a slow life-history pace characterized by delayed maturation and extended adult survival. In the wild, actual longevity is presumably shorter due to predation pressure from birds of prey, mammalian carnivores, and larger snakes, as well as the cumulative effects of environmental stochasticity and food limitation. Nevertheless, the species' capacity for prolonged somatic maintenance suggests a robust physiological resilience to oxidative stress and cellular senescence. The first reproductive event in these snakes occurs relatively late in life, with individuals typically engaging in their initial breeding activity at 4 years [tR = 4 years] of age after hatching under the same thermal regimen of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], a delay that reflects the extensive time required to attain the body size necessary for successful reproduction.

This species delays its initial breeding until four years after hatching [tR = four years after hatching], a prolonged pre-reproductive period that allows individuals to accumulate sufficient body reserves to support the high energetic demands of egg production in a seasonally constrained Mediterranean environment at a temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C]. During this pre-reproductive juvenile phase, individuals must accumulate enough energy reserves to support both continued growth and the eventual production of a clutch of yolk-laden eggs. The thermal dependence of these life-history transitions is critical: at the recommended maintenance temperature of 18 °C [T = 18 °C], metabolic rates are moderate, allowing for steady but not accelerated development. In cooler microhabitats, maturation could be delayed even further, while warmer conditions might hasten growth but also elevate maintenance costs. Interestingly, the estimated maximum adult wet weight of 1678 grams [Wwi = 1678 grams] aligns well with the asymptotic body lengths, indicating that both sexes achieve a robust, muscular physique suited for active pursuit of lizards, small mammals, and occasionally birds. This weight value, extrapolated from Thamnophis gigas due to their similar overall body proportions, provides a useful benchmark for future morphometric studies on Hierophis viridiflavus.
